Posted September 24, 2007 

Analysis by Richard Cowan  

 

Last nights 60 Minutes segment on medical marijuana dispensaries in Los Angeles, The Debate On California's Pot Shops, was just more evidence of my thesis that the best two-word explanation of marijuana prohibition is bad journalism.  

For another example from CBS, see 

European Study Shows Potency of Prohibitionist Propaganda. CBS and The AP Lie to the American People About the Dutch. Surprise!  

 

And it brought back a few odd memories. 

 

In November of 1994, when I was still National Director of NORML, I was interviewed by Morley Safer outside of Amsterdams Pax Party House, during the Cannabis Cup. The interview never ran on 60 Minutes, but that surreal scene still can give us some insight into the workings of journalism. I wrote about it once before in 1998
See 

Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments. 

 

The more things change 

 

This 60 Minutes report does not question that there is a need for medical marijuana. It includes statements by patients, who appear credible, some clearly in bad health. There is no indication that these people might have a problem getting medicine, instead, the problem is that it's time for the federal government to step in and legalize and properly control medical marijuana. 

 

That was the Washington Posts position in 1999! 

See 

Tale of Two Capital City Newspapers:  

The Washington Post and The Ottawa Citizen On Medical Marijuana  

-- Maybe We Should Apologize To King George. 

 

If, as the report concedes, cannabis really does have medical value, then shouldnt the primary concern of any decent society be the well-being of the patients, not the preservation of prohibition?  And why isnt news that patients are still being arrested in even California and other states with medical marijuana laws? 

   

And why, given the federal governments long history of lying about cannabis, should the patients have any faith in the governments ability to provide good medicine. 

See

More Proof That The Drug War Is Really A War On Cannabis. Plus: Sabotaging Medical Cannabis Research And Lying About It. Analysis by Richard Cowan



 

But there is no mention of these facts and here is their premise: 

 

A decade ago, California became the first of a dozen states in the nation to legalize medical marijuana. True believers, including many doctors, say pot works to ease pain or counter the side effects of chemotherapy. And the NationalAcademy of Sciences agrees, if the drug is carefully used. Critics see medical use as the gateway to legalizing all marijuana.  

 

First, notice the term true believers. That is usual used to describe religious and/or political extremists.  

 

Second, the reference to the National Academy of Sciences presumably means the 1999 Institute of Medicine report, which said However, except for the harms associated with smoking, the adverse effects of marijuana use are within the range of effects tolerated for other medicine. 

   

As we have seen many times, the IOM report emphasized the supposed risks of smoking and ignored the fact that cannabis does not have to be smoked.  

See 

No Medicine Is Smoked. Okay, But Why Isnt Cannabis Sold Over-the-Counter? New MAPS/NORML Vaporizer Study Undermines Key Part Of Prohibitionist Party Line On Smoked-Marijuana.  

 

Inasmuch as cannabis has no risk of overdose, in 1988 Drug Enforcement Administration Administrative Law Judge, Francis Young, called cannabis "One of the safest therapeutically active substances known....",  

See 

Bushs New Freedom Initiative: Treatment For Using Cannabis, From The Wonderful Folks Who Brought Us Vioxx, Baycol, Etc. Author of IOM Report Says, "I can't understand why it isn't rescheduled."

 

Third, CBS states the prohibitionist view as, Critics see medical use as the gateway to legalizing all marijuana. That is only partially correct. It is the official position of the Federal government that marijuana has no medical value.  

See 

Reading Between The Lies. New Version of An Old Lie About My Saying Medical Cannabis Is A Scam May Be Clue to New Prohibitionist Party Line. Only A Few Hundred Patients?  

and
Never Mind What HHS Says Now About Medical Marijuana, Here Is What The DEA Says. And No One Could Reasonably Be Expected To Trust A Government That Lies Like This. 

 

There is so much more that 60 Minutes might have said.  

 

Instead, they ask and answer the wrong question: 

Well, how is the California state law working? As correspondent Morley Safer reports, the answer involves another statute: the law of unintended consequences.  

See 

Unintended Consequences: How The Iraq War Has Changed the Global Climate for Cannabis Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan



 

For one thing, the federal government still views marijuana, medical or otherwise, as illegal and has been cracking down on dispensaries that sell it. For another, it's clear there are legions of people buying medical marijuana for the sole purpose of getting high. And for them and the truly ill in California, it's become an easy matter: just drop by your little pot shop around the corner.  

 

In many dispensaries up and down the state, there's a tasting corner, where you can sample the wares, and where you'll find any number of satisfied customers. 

 

Again, this gives the impression that there is easy (too easy) access to medical marijuana up and down the state. Unfortunately, that is untrue. If 60 Minutes wanted a real story they might have reported on how law enforcement in much of the state still ignores the legal rights of patients, violating state law.  

 

The most perverse twist to their report was their use of Scott Imler as their authority. It is a standard journalistic gimmick to give the appearance of objectivity by interviewing someone used to be in favor of whatever, but now has second thoughts. 

 

Rather than call someone who used to be opposed to medical marijuana, and is now in favor of it, they dredged up Imler. Oddly, they do not report anything about Imlers background. 

 

For openers, they do not report that Imler once ran a club much bigger than any that they report on, and it was raided by the DEA in 2001.  

 

Nor do they report that Imler was given only one years probation in 2003, while Todd McCormick was given 5 years, just for growing, and Peter McWilliams died because he was deprived of cannabis while he was awaiting trial.  

See
The Murder of Peter McWilliams -- An Indictment, Not an Obituary  by Richard Cowan  

and 

LA Weekly Looks Into How The Peter McWilliams Arrest Happened. Sounds Like LA Confidential 

Now Imler is just a reverend: 

"It's just ridiculous the amount of money that's going through these cannabis clubs. It's absolutely ridiculous," says Scott Imler, a minister in the UnitedMethodistChurch who has long been active in promoting medical marijuana.  

 

Peter McWilliams told me that the high prices charged by Imler were a major impetus to his fatal decision to get involved in medical marijuana growing. 

See 

Applications By California Groups To Grow Marijuana For The Feds  

Show How Weird Things Really Are  See The Punch Line at The End 

 

They set him up as the disillusioned idealist: 

Eleven years ago, he was working to pass proposition 215, the ballot measure that legalized it. Today, Imler has second thoughts.

 

 Having run one of the largest clubs of its time, Imler now says, 

"The purpose of proposition 215 was not to create a new industry. It was to protect legitimate patients from criminal prosecution."  

 

How can millions of patients be supplied with medicine that remains contraband under state law when it is not medical and therefore sells for almost the price of gold  even today  without creating a new industry? It is absurd to think that the sick and dying, often impoverished by illness, could grow their own. Consequently, the clubs  like Imlers  quickly emerged as the only workable solution in the context of prohibition. That is why they are still there today. 

 

60 minutes claims, 

The aim back then, reflected in television spots, was for a highly regulated system in which licensed pharmacies would dispense medical marijuana to the seriously ill. Proposition 215's backers had people with AIDS, cancer, and glaucoma in mind.  

 

Certainly no one thought that Prop 215 was a permanent solution, but nothing in the text of the initiative suggested a highly regulated system in which licensed pharmacies would dispense medical marijuana. That would have required a change in federal law, which was actually encouraged as follows: 

To encourage the federal and state governments to implement a plan to provide for the safe and affordable distribution of marijuana to all patients in medical need of marijuana. 

See

Full Text of Proposition 215 Compassionate Use Act of 1996  

 

The state has not done enough to enforce its own laws and the federal government has opposed these aims since the day after 215 won, so the system evolved to deal with the real world.. 

 

As for 215 covering disease other than AIDS, cancer, and glaucoma, 60 Minutes gives the impression that this was somehow a flaw, and unique to medical marijuana. 

 

Imler claims: 

"What happened when we were writing it was, as you can imagine, every patient group in the state and they all have their lobbies. You know, the kidney patients and the heart patient. Every patient group wanted to be included in the list," Imler recalls. "And so we didn't wanna get in the position of deciding what it could be used for and what it couldn't be used for. We weren't doctors. We weren't scientists. We weren't researchers. We were just patients with a problem."  

 

Imler says they were forced to make the proposition vague.  

 

So the law voters passed mentioned not only cancer and AIDS but "...any other illness for which marijuana provides relief." A decade later, if youve got a note from a doctor, you can buy medical pot for just about any imaginable condition.  

 

In fact, the only ambiguity in the initiative was in the supply chain. The inclusion of "...any other illness for which marijuana provides relief" is not ambiguous. Nor is it unique to medical marijuana. 

 

Under the US prescription system, doctors can prescribe any Schedule 3 drug for "...any other illness for which it  provides relief. It is called off-label use.    

 

As it happens, Marinol, (synthetic THC) is now in Schedule 3. And is commonly prescribed off-label to those who can afford it. 

See 

Kubby to Return to Jail. Survival Depends on Marinol. Two and Half Years Probation to Follow. Triumph of Prosecutorial State. Special to MarijuanaNews.
and 

Marinol Was The First Schedule 2 Drug To Be "Down-Scheduled,"

Boasts Roxanne On Its New Marinol.com Web Site.

Doesnt That Mean That It Should Never Have Been Schedule 2 Anyway?

and
A Medical Marijuana User Says That "Marinol Rescheduling Is Worthless" For Him. He Simply Cannot Afford It. "My country is killing me." 

 

"Let me just ask you plain and simple. Is there this proliferation because people are simply using, quote, unquote, medical marijuana, to get high?" Safer asks.  

 

"I think there's a lot of that. And I think you know, a lot of what we have now is basically pot dealers in storefronts," Imler says.  

 

What year in divinity school did the Rev. Imler learn to judge the motives of others?  

 

However, there is no doubt that there is leakage from the medical marijuana system. 

 

Television station KCBS went to a Los Angeles clinic, where the waiting room was full of young people, joking about what they'd tell the doctor their ailment was.  

 

It is interesting to recall, as Morley Safer apparently does not, that when Al Gore III was arrested last July for speeding in his Prius, he had, without a prescription, Adderall, Vicodin, Xanax and Valium  and less than an ounce of marijuana.   

 

Gores crime was hardly unique. 

 

On September 6, Reuters reported that the government's annual report on substance abuse found that non-medical use of prescription drugs, mostly pain relievers, among young adults increased from 5.4 percent in 2002 to 6.4 percent in 2006.  

 

Recently, the Partnership for a Drug Free Americas annual tracking study found 

1 in 5 teens has abused a prescription pain medication  

1 in 5 report abusing prescription stimulants and tranquilizers  

1 in 10 has abused cough medication 

 

Interestingly, current marijuana use among those ages 12 to 17 dropped from 8.2 percent in 2002 to 6.7 percent in 2006, with the decline seen particularly among boys.  

 

Moreover, according to a 2004 report, the number of California ninth graders reporting marijuana use in the last 30 days declined by 47% from 1996 (when Prop 215 passed) to 2004. 

 

Does that indicate that leakage from the medical marijuana system is a problem that should be of concern to anyone? 

 

Two points here. 

 

First, teen marijuana use has dropped while anyone can supposedly get it in California, and prescription drug abuse has risen. 

See  

John Walters Says, Prescription Drug Abuse Is The Second Largest Illicit Drug Problem  After Cannabis, Of Course! Different Measures for Success and Failure. Seeking New Victims.

 

Second, isnt it better that recreational users buy cannabis from the medical dispensaries, rather than from street dealers, who may also sell hard drugs? 

 

In fairness to 60 Minutes, they also interviewed Don Duncan, who has two dispensaries  he had three until the Feds raided one shortly after Safers interview. 

 

Duncan did an excellent job. (He is also an activist and is on the board of directors of Americans for Safe Access.)  

 

Duncan explained,  

Theres bound to be abuse in the system. You know, our pharmacies are abused by people who want to abuse prescription drugs. And so it's reasonable to assume that our medical cannabis facilities are abused as well. What we really need right now are regulations that address those issues.   

 

But Safer was more than happy to let Imler to pontificate further. 

 

"Most of these cannabis centers are buying their marijuana off the black market. Theyre dumping millions of dollars into the criminal black market," Imler says.  

 

Of course, all cannabis in DEAland comes from the criminal black market as far as the Federal government is concerned.  

 

"Marijuana - what? Coming in from Mexico or wherever?" Safer asks.  

 

"Some of it is," Imler says. "Some of these places sell hashish, which comes in from the BeccaValley in Lebanon."  

 

There is really no way that Imler could know that. Hash also comes from Morocco, Afghanistan, Nepal, and from California. But so what? That is an artifact of prohibition not of medical marijuana. 

 

And looking back on a decade of controversy, Rev. Scott Imler concedes that good Samaritans with good intentions weren't enough. He argues it's time for the federal government to step in and legalize and properly control medical marijuana.  

 

"Until that happens, were gonna have what we have now, which is chaos," he says.  

 

On the contrary, it is time for the federal government to get out of the way and leave any regulation to the states. Some regulation, such as age restrictions, is inevitable, but I have no desire to see the geniuses of Baghdad and Katrina pushing Mississippi schwag on the patients and then arresting anyone who threatens their monopoly. 

 

And as for what we have now being chaos Well, it is a partially free market. Cannabis prohibition is the real chaos. 

See

The Theory and Practice of Chaos  Analysis By Richard Cowan
